newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Iscor Saldanha project on track.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Iscor Saldanha project on track.

text.p: Construction of South Africa's much-delayed Saldanha Steel project was now on track and should meet its target of swinging into production in the first half of 1998, project director Ben Nel said on Wednesday.

Initially delayed by environmental concerns and labour unrest, the 6.5 billion rand joint venture by Iscor Ltd and the state's Industrial Development Corporation now had 4,700 construction workers on site and was about 52 percent complete, Nel told Reuters.

"It is still our programme to start the first production on the steel-making side in the latter part of the first half of next year and for the iron-making side to start in the last quarter of next year," Nel said.
Nel said the initial output of the project would be about 250,000 tonnes but Saldanha Steel could expand the plant in future to double capacity.

He said there were about 70 contractors on site from all over the country with the biggest being a joint venture between LTA Ltd, Group Five Ltd, Groenewalds and Dorbyl Ltd which was building the steel plant itself.
The project would use the low-cost Corex process, which was cleaner than conventional iron making processes, together with a direct reduce iron (DRI) plant.
This would ensure that all the iron was produced in pressure vessels which did not emit fumes into the atmosphere.
"All the impurities will go out in a slag to a slag dump where it will be solidified in a glass form so that it cannot leach into the ground," Nel said.
This would prevent any pollution of underground water tables, a major concern of local environmentalists who initially opposed the plant.
This delayed the start-up of the project, which is now being monitored by a special environmental committee appointed by the Western Cape government.

The project would use iron ore from Iscor's Sishen mine in Northern Province and most of the steel produced would be exported. Marketing agreements were being negotiated to South East Asia and the Middle East.
"But we have been talking to a Swiss based company, DuFerco, and the Industrial Development Corporation, who want to put up downstream facilities," Nel said.
"Those negotiations are very near to conclusion and should be wrapped up in the next couple of weeks."
The steel plant will be powered by electricity but Nel said that future expansion plans could involve the use of gas from Namibia's Kudu gas fields, should they be developed by then.
Portnet's 82 million rand project to upgrade Saldanha Bay to handle imports and exports from the steel project was also on target.
"They have almost completed blasting operations for the new quay and last week they started dredging the port and constructing the pre-caste sections for the quay itself," Nel said.
